chief_complaint: dry cough for 10 days after cold, normal chest exam
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with dry cough for 10 days after cold, normal chest exam. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the cold settled deep in her lungs and might have turned into a mild case of pneumonia.
concerns: She is worried that the persistent coughing fits will keep her awake and leave her too exhausted to look after her granddaughter this weekend.
expectations: She hopes to get a prescription for a strong cough syrup or an antibiotic to finally soothe her chest and clear the cough.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Viral Cough (Acute Bronchitis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Viral Cough (Acute Bronchitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes symptomatic care and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics (Choosing Wisely), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dry cough for 10 days after cold, normal chest exam

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with dry cough for 10 days after cold, normal chest exam. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Normal vital signs, no fever, clear lung fields on auscultation with no wheezes, crackles, or focal findings.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Viral Cough (Acute Bronchitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever, focal findings.
management_principles: Plan for Post-Viral Cough: Choosing Wisely: avoid antibiotics
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of dry cough for 10 days after cold, normal chest exam. HPI: Persistent dry cough for 10 days following an upper respiratory infection, no fever, no shortness of breath.
reference_soap.objective: Normal vital signs, no fever, clear lung fields on auscultation with no wheezes, crackles, or focal findings.
reference_soap.assessment: Post-viral cough (acute bronchitis), given a normal chest exam and absence of fever or focal findings that would suggest pneumonia.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Post-Viral Cough: Choosing Wisely: avoid antibiotics. Honey, OTC dextromethorphan. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Post-Viral Cough
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Post-Viral Cough
Implement evidence-based management plan: Choosing Wisely: avoid antibiotics. Honey, OTC dextromethorphan

teaching.one_liner: A dry cough persisting after a cold, with a normal chest exam, managed with symptomatic relief rather than antibiotics.

must_ask.say: Did this start after a cold?
Is the cough dry or productive?

history.answer: I've had this nagging dry cough for the past ten days, ever since I had a cold.
It started about ten days ago and has been gradually getting worse.
About two weeks ago I caught a common cold with a runny nose and scratchy throat, which cleared up right before this cough began.
No, I rarely get sick and I've never had a persistent cough like this before.
It is completely dry and hacking. I'm not bringing up any phlegm or mucus at all.
It bothers me throughout the day, but it tends to get worse in the evening and when I lie down in bed.
I get coughing fits where I cough several times in a row, but there's no whooping sound and I've never vomited from it.
Breathing in cold air or talking for a long time tickles my throat and triggers the cough.
No, I haven't heard any whistling or wheezing sounds, and I don't feel short of breath.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills at all.
No, there has never been any blood when I cough.
No, my weight has been completely stable and I don't have night sweats.
My chest muscles feel a little sore from all the coughing, but there is no sharp pain when I breathe in.
The runny nose from my cold went away a week ago, and I don't feel anything dripping down the back of my throat.
No, I don't have heartburn, acid regurgitation, or any sour taste in my mouth.
No, I can lie flat without trouble, and my legs are not swollen.
I don't take any blood pressure medications like ACE inhibitors, or any prescription pills.
My young grandson had a head cold a couple of weeks ago, but no one at home has an ongoing cough.
No, I have never had tuberculosis and I have never been exposed to anyone who had it.
I am a retired homemaker, and our home is clean with no mold, dust, birds, or chemical fumes.
No, I have never had asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis.
I've been feeling quite worn out and tired, mostly because the coughing wakes me up at night.
I was thinking that bad cold might have settled deep in my chest and turned into pneumonia.
I'm really worried that this coughing will wear me out completely so I won't have the energy to watch my granddaughter this weekend.
I'm hoping you can prescribe a strong cough medicine or an antibiotic so I can finally get rid of this tickle and sleep.
I have always been healthy and don't have any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any regular prescription medicines, over-the-counter remedies, or supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only have a small glass of wine once or twice a month at social gatherings.
I am retired and live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no family history of chronic lung conditions, asthma, or lung cancer.
I went through menopause more than ten years ago.

exam.finding: Patient is alert and in no acute distress, with occasional dry coughing during the examination.
Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Nasal mucosa is normal without discharge or swelling; pharynx is clear without erythema, exudate, or post-nasal drip.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Symmetric chest expansion with normal tactile fremitus and no chest wall tenderness.
Resonant percussion note bilaterally throughout all lung fields.
Vesicular breath sounds clear bilaterally without wheezes, crackles, rhonchi, or focal changes.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
No peripheral edema in the lower extremities, and no digital clubbing.
